prompt: The pamphlet's chart shows Midpier's bar towering over Northport's. Look at the value axis. What does the chart actually show?

visual.caption: Crates landed at five ports, drawn from 47
visual.accessibleDescription: Bar chart of crates landed at five ports with the value axis starting at 47, not zero. Northport 48, Eastquay 50, Southbar 51, Westhead 52, Midpier 53 — so the bars rise 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 above the axis and Midpier's appears six times the height of Northport's.

choices.text: A difference of 5 crates between 48 and 53, drawn from an axis starting at 47
Midpier landing about six times as many crates as Northport
Figures that must be wrong, since the bars disagree with the labels

hints.text: Find where the numbers on the left-hand axis begin.
The bars measure from 47, not from zero. What is 53 minus 48?

explanation: Northport landed 48 crates and Midpier 53 — a difference of 5, about a tenth. The axis starts at 47, so the bars show 1 and 6 rather than 48 and 53, and Midpier's looks six times the height. Every figure on the chart is correct. What is wrong is the impression, and it comes entirely from where the axis begins.
solutionSteps: Read the value axis: it starts at 47 crates, not at zero.
Read the two figures: Northport 48, Midpier 53.
The bars therefore rise 1 and 6 above the axis, a ratio of 6 from a real difference of 5 crates.
accessibilityDescription: A bar chart of five ports drawn from a value axis starting at 47; three readings of what it shows.

prompt: This is the same season drawn from zero. How many more crates did Midpier land than Northport?

visual.caption: Crates landed at five ports, drawn from zero
visual.accessibleDescription: Bar chart of crates landed at five ports with the value axis starting at zero: Northport 48, Eastquay 50, Southbar 51, Westhead 52, Midpier 53. The five bars are close to level.

hints.text: Read both bars against the axis, then subtract.

explanation: Midpier landed 53 crates and Northport 48, so the difference is 5. Drawn from zero the five bars are close to level, which is what a season of 48 to 53 crates looks like. The pamphlet's chart contains these same two numbers.
accessibilityDescription: A bar chart of five ports drawn from zero; enter how many more crates Midpier landed than Northport.

prompt: Here are the twenty channel soundings again, this time in two bins ten metres wide instead of five bins four metres wide. What has the wider bin width done?

visual.caption: Channel soundings, bins 10 metres wide
visual.accessibleDescription: Histogram of the same twenty channel soundings in two wide bins: 2 up to 12 metres holds 11 soundings and 12 up to 22 holds 9. The season looks like a single plain lump.

choices.text: Smoothed the season into one plain lump, hiding where the soundings actually cluster
Discarded some soundings, since two bins cannot hold what five did
Made the chart wrong, because four-metre bins are the correct width for this data

explanation: All twenty soundings are still there — 11 in the lower bin and 9 in the upper. What is gone is the shape: the five-bin chart showed the readings peaking between 6 and 10 metres and thinning towards the deep end, and two wide bins flatten that into a near-even pair. Neither width is 'correct'. Both are honest drawings, and a reader who is not told the bin width cannot tell which story they are being shown.
accessibilityDescription: A histogram of twenty soundings in two wide bins; three readings of what the wider bins did.

prompt: Explain in your own words how a chart can contain no false number and still mislead, and name two things to check before believing one. Use the words 'axis' and 'true'.
explanation: Every value on a chart can be true while its construction carries a false impression: a value axis starting above zero turns a tenth into a sixfold gap, and a bin width chosen for effect can smooth away a cluster or manufacture spikes. Both are decisions invisible in the finished picture. Checking where the axis starts and what the intervals are catches most of it, and neither check requires assuming the author meant to deceive.
accessibilityDescription: An open-response question about how an accurate chart can mislead and what to check first.

prompt: On the pamphlet's chart the axis starts at 47, so Northport's bar rises 1 and Midpier's rises 6. How many times taller does Midpier's bar appear than Northport's?

visual.caption: Crates landed at five ports, drawn from 47
visual.accessibleDescription: Bar chart of crates landed at five ports with the value axis starting at 47, not zero. Northport 48, Eastquay 50, Southbar 51, Westhead 52, Midpier 53 — so the bars rise 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6 above the axis and Midpier's appears six times the height of Northport's.

hints.text: Compare the two heights above the axis, not the two landing figures.

explanation: Six divided by one is 6, so Midpier's bar appears six times the height of Northport's. The landings themselves differ by a factor of about 1.1. That gap between 6 and 1.1 is the whole effect of the truncated axis, and it is produced without a single incorrect number.
accessibilityDescription: The truncated bar chart; enter how many times taller Midpier's bar appears than Northport's.

prompt: Two channels both have a median depth of 10 metres. Channel A's middle half spans 0.3 metres and Channel B's spans 2.6. Which is the more predictable channel?

choices.text: Channel A - its middle half sits within a much narrower band of depths
Neither - they share a median, so they behave the same way
Channel B - a wider middle half means more soundings were taken

hints.text: The medians agree. What does the width of each middle half tell you beyond that?
Half of every channel's soundings fall inside its middle half. Which band is narrower?

explanation: Half of Channel A's soundings fall within 0.3 metres, so a skipper meets much the same depth every night. Half of Channel B's are spread across 2.6 metres, and the outer quarters go further still. The shared median says the two middles agree and says nothing whatever about that difference.
solutionSteps: Note what the medians tell you: both channels sit around 10 metres in the middle.
Compare the middle halves: A spans 0.3 metres, B spans 2.6.
The narrower band is the more predictable channel, so Channel A.
accessibilityDescription: Two channels sharing a median but differing in the width of their middle halves; choose the more predictable one.

prompt: Channel A has a first quartile of 9.85 metres and a third of 10.15. Channel B, shown here, has a first quartile of 7 and a third of 14.5. How much wider is Channel B's middle half, in metres?

visual.caption: Channel B, five-number summary
visual.accessibleDescription: Box plot of Channel B's twenty soundings: smallest 2 metres, first quartile 7, median 10.5, third quartile 14.5, largest 22. The box spans 7 to 14.5 metres.

hints.text: Work out each channel's interquartile range first, then subtract.

explanation: Channel A's middle half spans 10.15 - 9.85 = 0.3 metres and Channel B's spans 14.5 - 7 = 7.5, so B's is 7.2 metres wider. Comparing spread means computing the same measure on both sets and then setting the two against one another — not reading one and guessing at the other.
accessibilityDescription: A box plot of Channel B and quartiles for Channel A; enter how much wider B's middle half is, in metres.

prompt: A report states that two harbours had the same mean wait for a berth last season, and concludes that the two run equally well. What is missing?

choices.text: The spread and the shape - one harbour could be steady while the other swings between minutes and hours
Nothing - equal means is what it means for two harbours to run equally well
The number of boats, since a mean says nothing about how many waited

hints.text: A mean is one number standing for a whole season. What does standing for a season give up?

explanation: Two harbours with the same mean wait can be entirely different places: one where nearly every skipper waits about that long, and one where most are seen at once and a few wait half a day. The mean is identical and the experience is not. A comparison needs the spread and the shape beside it before any claim about how the two run is worth making.
accessibilityDescription: Three accounts of what is missing from a comparison of two harbours based only on their mean wait.

prompt: A surveyor compares two channels by drawing a box plot of each, but scales the two charts to fill their own frames. Why is that comparison unsafe?

choices.text: On different scales the eye compares picture sizes rather than depths, so a narrow channel can look as varied as a wide one
Box plots cannot be used for comparison; only histograms can
Five numbers are too few to compare two channels with

explanation: Box plots are built for comparison, and the comparison lives in their positions and widths against a shared scale. Give each its own scale and both boxes fill their frames whatever their depths, so a channel varying by a third of a metre draws exactly like one varying by three. Every number is correct; the pictures are not comparable, which is the same failure a truncated axis makes.
accessibilityDescription: Three critiques of comparing two channels with box plots drawn on separate scales.

prompt: Explain in your own words why two datasets sharing a median can still be worth telling apart, and what you would ask for next. Use the words 'centre' and 'spread'.
explanation: A median is a single value standing for a whole set, so two sets sharing one have agreed about their centre and about nothing else. They may differ in how far the readings reach, in how tightly the bulk holds together, and in whether either has a long tail. The next thing to ask for is the spread — an interquartile range or a range — and then the shape, because a set with an outlier and one without can match on both centre and spread.
accessibilityDescription: An open-response question about why a shared median leaves two datasets worth telling apart.

prompt: Channel A: median 10, interquartile range 0.3, mean 10. Channel B: median 10, interquartile range 0.3, mean 13. Both were sounded twenty times. What does the evidence support?

choices.text: Their middles and middle halves match, but B's mean sitting above its median says B has a long tail of deep soundings
The two channels are the same, since the median and the interquartile range both agree
Channel B is uniformly deeper, because its mean is higher

hints.text: Two of the three comparisons agree. Look at what the third one says.
A mean well above a median is the signature of a tail on which side?

explanation: Centre and spread both match, which is exactly the case where a comparison stopping at two measures would report the channels as identical. The mean is the third reading: B's sits 3 metres above its median while A's sits on it, and a mean above the median means a long tail on the high side. B is not uniformly deeper — most of it matches A — it has a handful of much deeper soundings pulling its mean up. That is the shape, and it is the part only the third comparison found.
accessibilityDescription: Two channels agreeing on median and interquartile range but not on mean; choose what the evidence supports.
